blocks.html: The problem. We want a deep generative model: a neural network that, after seeing a pile of images, can invent new ones and also explain each image with a compact code. The natural recipe is a latent-variable model — assume each image $x$ was produced from some hidden vector $z$ (think: 'digit identity', 'slant', 'stroke thickness') — and then train it by maximizing the likelihood of the data. The trouble is that doing this exactly requires the posterior $p_\theta(z\mid x)$ (given an image, what hidden code produced it?), and for any interesting neural decoder that posterior is intractable: it involves an integral with no closed form.

The intuition. Variational inference's old answer was: approximate the nasty posterior with a simpler distribution $q(z)$ and optimize it — per datapoint, with its own inner optimization loop. On a million images that is hopelessly slow. The VAE's key move is amortization: train one encoder network $q_\phi(z\mid x)$ that, in a single forward pass, outputs an approximate posterior for any input. The cost of inference is 'amortized' across the whole dataset — you pay once to train the encoder, then inference is free.

The two contributions, stated plainly. (1) A reparameterization of the variational lower bound that yields a simple, low-variance estimator you can optimize with ordinary stochastic gradient descent — the Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes (SGVB) estimator. (2) For i.i.d. datasets with continuous latents, fitting an approximate inference model (the encoder) to the intractable posterior makes inference itself efficient. Together these turn a thorny Bayesian problem into a standard backprop training loop.

The analogy. A VAE is an autoencoder with a probabilistic conscience. A plain autoencoder squeezes $x$ into a code and reconstructs it. The VAE adds two demands: the code must be a distribution (not a single point), and that distribution must stay close to a fixed simple prior $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. That second demand is what makes the latent space smooth and the model genuinely generative — you can sample a code from the prior and get a plausible new image.

Context. Published at ICLR 2014, this paper (with Rezende, Mohamed & Wierstra's contemporaneous work) made deep latent-variable models trainable at scale and seeded a huge family — conditional VAEs, β-VAE, VQ-VAE, NVAE — and conceptually anticipated diffusion models, the next paper in this collection.

sections.title: 2. Method — the model and the problem

pages.title: The generative story and three things we want

blocks.html: The generative story. The paper posits a simple two-step process behind every datapoint. First draw a latent $z^{(i)}$ from a prior $p_\theta(z)$; then draw the observation $x^{(i)}$ from a conditional $p_\theta(x\mid z)$. Both are parameterized by neural networks with shared parameters $\theta$. The latent $z$ is never observed — we only ever see $x$.

Reading it. $p_\theta(z)$ is the prior, almost always a standard Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ — a 'blank canvas' of independent unit-variance dimensions. $p_\theta(x\mid z)$ is the decoder (a.k.a. the likelihood or generative network): a neural net that turns a code $z$ into the parameters of a distribution over $x$ (e.g. Bernoulli probabilities for black-and-white pixels, or a Gaussian mean for grayscale). $\theta$ are the decoder weights.
The intractabilities the paper highlights. Two integrals stand in the way:

items: The marginal likelihood $p_\theta(x)=\int p_\theta(x\mid z)p_\theta(z)\,dz$ — needed to train by maximum likelihood — has no closed form for a neural decoder.
The true posterior $p_\theta(z\mid x)=p_\theta(x\mid z)p_\theta(z)/p_\theta(x)$ — needed to infer the code for a given image — is therefore also intractable.
Large datasets make matters worse: per-datapoint inference loops (sampling-based EM, mean-field VB) are too slow when you have hundreds of thousands of examples.

blocks.html: The three target problems. The paper frames its solution as solving (1) efficient maximum-likelihood estimation of $\theta$; (2) efficient approximate posterior inference of $z$ given $x$ (useful for coding, denoising, representation learning); and (3) efficient approximate inference of the marginal $p_\theta(x)$, useful wherever a prior over $x$ is needed. One trick will address all three.

pages.title: The variational lower bound (ELBO), term by term

blocks.html: The goal. We cannot maximize $\log p_\theta(x)$ directly. Variational inference's classic workaround is to introduce the encoder $q_\phi(z\mid x)$ and derive a lower bound on the log-likelihood that we can compute and maximize. Push the bound up and you push the true likelihood up with it.
The exact decomposition. For any choice of $q_\phi$, the marginal log-likelihood splits into two non-negative-gapped pieces:

Reading it. The first term is the KL divergence between the encoder's guess and the true posterior — it is $\geq 0$ and measures how wrong our approximation is. The second term $\mathcal{L}$ is the variational (evidence) lower bound, the ELBO. Because the KL term is non-negative, $\log p_\theta(x^{(i)}) \geq \mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x^{(i)})$, with equality exactly when the encoder matches the true posterior.
The form we actually optimize. The ELBO rearranges into a clean, interpretable pair of terms:

items: Reconstruction term $\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)]$: encode $x$ to a code $z$, decode it, and reward the model when the decoder assigns high probability to the original $x$. This is the 'autoencoder' part — it wants faithful reconstructions.

KL regularizer $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z))$: punish the encoder when its per-image posterior drifts far from the prior $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. This keeps the latent space packed, smooth, and samplable — it stops the encoder from cheating by spreading each image into its own private, far-flung region of latent space.

blocks.html: Why two competing terms. Reconstruction alone would let the model memorize: assign every image a unique spike in latent space and copy it back perfectly, leaving the space full of holes you cannot sample from. The KL term is the counter-pressure that forces codes to overlap and tile the prior, which is precisely what lets you draw $z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ at generation time and get something sensible. The whole art of training VAEs is balancing this tension (β-VAE later turns the balance into an explicit knob).

pages.title: The SGVB estimator and the AEVB algorithm

blocks.html: The remaining obstacle. The reconstruction term is an expectation over $q_\phi(z\mid x)$, i.e. it requires sampling $z$. A naive Monte-Carlo gradient with respect to the encoder parameters $\phi$ — using the score-function / REINFORCE estimator — has notoriously high variance, so high that gradient descent crawls or stalls. We need a low-variance way to differentiate through the sampling step.

The SGVB estimator. Once we can draw $z$ as a differentiable function of $\phi$ and noise (the reparameterization on the next page), the ELBO becomes a plain Monte-Carlo average we can backprop through:

Reading it. $L$ is the number of latent samples drawn per datapoint; the paper notes that as long as the minibatch is reasonably large (they use $M=100$), $L=1$ is enough — a single sample per image. The KL term is often available in closed form (e.g. Gaussian-to-Gaussian, shown next page), so only the reconstruction term is sampled.
The AEVB algorithm (the training loop). The paper's Algorithm 1, Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes, is refreshingly ordinary once the trick is in place:

items: Sample a minibatch of $M$ datapoints from the dataset.
Compute the gradient $\nabla_{\theta,\phi}\tilde{\mathcal{L}}$ of the minibatch estimator (one backward pass through encoder and decoder together).
Update $\theta$ and $\phi$ with an SGD-style optimizer (the paper uses Adagrad). Repeat until convergence.

blocks.html: Why this was a breakthrough. A problem that previously demanded per-datapoint variational optimization or MCMC now trains exactly like a regular deep net: one objective, one set of joint parameters $(\theta,\phi)$, standard minibatch gradient descent. That is what made deep latent-variable models practical.

The core problem in one sentence. You cannot backpropagate through a coin flip. The ELBO needs $z\sim q_\phi(z\mid x)$, but a random draw has no derivative with respect to the parameters $\phi$ that shaped the distribution — the sampling node blocks the gradient.

The trick / the analogy. Move the randomness out of the way. Instead of letting the network sample $z$ directly, draw a fixed, parameter-free noise variable $\epsilon$ from a standard Gaussian, and then build $z$ as a deterministic, differentiable function of $\epsilon$ and the encoder's outputs. The randomness now lives in $\epsilon$ (which has nothing to learn), while $\mu$ and $\sigma$ — the things we want gradients for — sit on a smooth, differentiable path. Think of it as routing the dice roll around the part of the circuit that needs to be differentiable.

Reading every symbol. The encoder outputs a mean vector $\mu_\phi(x)$ and a (diagonal) standard-deviation vector $\sigma_\phi(x)$ for the input $x$. $\epsilon$ is sampled fresh from $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and carries no learnable parameters. $\odot$ is elementwise multiplication. The result $z$ is distributed exactly as $\mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi,\sigma_\phi^2)$ — but now $\partial z/\partial \mu$ and $\partial z/\partial \sigma$ are well-defined, so gradients flow from the reconstruction loss back into the encoder.

The Gaussian KL in closed form. Because both $q_\phi(z\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)$ and the prior $p_\theta(z)=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ are Gaussian, the KL term needs no sampling at all — the paper gives it analytically for a $J$-dimensional latent:

Reading it. Summed over the $J$ latent dimensions, this term is largest (least negative) when each $\mu_j\to 0$ and $\sigma_j\to 1$ — i.e. when the encoder's posterior is the standard normal prior. It explicitly penalizes means that wander from zero and variances that stray from one, which is the regularizing pressure that keeps the latent space tidy.

Why it works / what would break without it. This is the technical kernel of the entire paper. Without reparameterization, the encoder and decoder cannot be trained jointly by gradient descent — you would be stuck with high-variance score-function gradients. With it, the VAE collapses into an end-to-end-differentiable autoencoder that also happens to be a principled probabilistic model. A practical note: networks usually output $\log\sigma^2$ rather than $\sigma$ directly, so variances stay positive without constraints.

Putting the pieces together. Section 3 of the paper instantiates the whole framework as a concrete model — the one everyone now calls 'the VAE'. The prior is $p_\theta(z)=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$; the decoder $p_\theta(x\mid z)$ is an MLP (Bernoulli outputs for binary MNIST, Gaussian outputs for continuous data); and the encoder $q_\phi(z\mid x)$ is an MLP that outputs the $\mu$ and $\log\sigma^2$ of a diagonal Gaussian over $z$.
The Gaussian-encoder loss in full. With the analytic KL plugged in, the per-datapoint objective the paper maximizes is the sum of the closed-form KL and a sampled reconstruction term:

Reading it. The left sum is the negative KL pulling the posterior toward $\mathcal{N}(0,I)$; the right sum is the average reconstruction log-likelihood over $L$ reparameterized samples $z^{(i,l)}=\mu^{(i)}+\sigma^{(i)}\odot\epsilon^{(l)}$. Maximizing this single scalar trains encoder and decoder simultaneously.

How it relates to prior work. The paper's related-work section places the SGVB estimator against the wake-sleep algorithm (which optimizes two separate objectives and cannot match a single likelihood bound), and notes that the reparameterized estimator is what makes joint, single-objective training possible. The encoder playing the role of a learned, amortized recognition model is the conceptual bridge from classical variational inference to deep learning.

Common misconception. A VAE is not 'an autoencoder with added noise'. The noise, the KL term, and the probabilistic decoder are all derived from a single likelihood lower bound — the autoencoder structure is a consequence of the math, not the starting point. That is why VAEs give you a real generative model (sample the prior, decode) rather than just a compression scheme.

pages.title: MNIST, Frey Faces, and what the latent space buys you

blocks.html: The benchmarks. The VAE is evaluated on MNIST (handwritten digits) and the Frey Faces dataset (continuous-valued face images). Encoders and decoders are MLPs with a single hidden layer of 500 units, trained with Adagrad on minibatches of $M=100$, using $L=1$ sample per datapoint. They vary the latent dimensionality $N_z$ and compare the SGVB lower bound against the wake-sleep algorithm and a Monte-Carlo EM baseline.

The headline result. SGVB/AEVB optimizes the marginal-likelihood lower bound faster and to a higher value than wake-sleep across latent sizes, and crucially keeps converging as the dataset grows — because the per-step cost is independent of dataset size. On the full-likelihood comparison (estimated with a Monte-Carlo / MCEM procedure) AEVB is competitive while being far cheaper per update.

The qualitative payoff: a smooth latent space. The more memorable evidence is visual. Walking along a straight line between two latent codes produces a smooth morph through plausible images — a 3 gradually becoming an 8, or one face slowly turning into another. A 2-D latent space can be laid out as a grid and decoded into a continuous manifold of digits. This continuity is not an accident: it is exactly what the KL-to-prior term incentivizes by forcing nearby codes to overlap and tile the prior.

The famous limitation: blur. VAE samples tend to be slightly soft compared to GAN samples. The reason is principled: a Gaussian decoder is trained toward the mean of all plausible reconstructions for a given code, and the average of many sharp images is a blurry one. This 'blurriness vs. sharpness' contrast with GANs (the previous paper) is the defining trade-off of the two model families.

Why it mattered. The VAE was the first deep generative model that paired a continuous, structured latent space with a principled, scalable training objective. Both halves were necessary: latent structure gives you interpolation and controllable generation, and the SGVB objective gives you a way to actually fit it on real data. That combination spawned a large research family.

items: Conditional VAE (CVAE) — condition generation on a label or attribute, so you can ask for 'a 7' or 'a smiling face'.
β-VAE — multiply the KL term by a weight $\beta>1$ to encourage disentangled latent dimensions (each axis controls one factor like rotation or thickness).
VQ-VAE — replace the continuous code with a discrete codebook; its tokens underpin DALL·E, neural audio codecs, and the image/audio tokenizers used by modern multimodal LLMs.
Hierarchical VAEs (NVAE, very deep VAEs) — stack many latent layers to capture coarse-to-fine structure and rival GAN sample quality.

blocks.html: The line to diffusion models. A modern diffusion model (the next paper, DDPM) can be read as a deep hierarchical VAE with hundreds or thousands of latent timesteps and a fixed (rather than learned) inference network — the forward noising process plays the role of the encoder. The variational lower bound that DDPM optimizes is a direct descendant of the ELBO derived here. The conceptual lineage of much of modern generative modeling runs straight back to this 2013 paper.
